-0.46179,38.36405.desc: A clinic mapped in OpenStreetMap as offering fertility treatment. OpenStreetMap holds what somebody chose to map, so a country with few points here may be thinly mapped rather than thinly served. That is the reverse of the national registers alongside it, which are close to complete for one country and silent everywhere else. This layer is a cross-check and a source of leads, not a count.

31.23573,30.04439.name: The Learning Resource Complex (LRC)
31.23573,30.04439.company: Kasr Al Ainy Faculty of Medicine - Cairo University
31.23573,30.04439.desc: An organisation accredited by AAALAC International for its care and use of laboratory animals. Part of Kasr Al Ainy Faculty of Medicine - Cairo University. Accreditation is voluntary and paid for, so this is a list of organisations that chose to be inspected rather than a register of everyone doing the work. An organisation absent from it is not accredited; that says nothing about whether it uses animals. In several countries the largest users are absent for exactly that reason. The directory gives a city and country and no street address, so this point marks where the organisation is registered rather than the building where animals are held.

-73.67284,45.48758.name: Human Health Therapeutics Ottawa
-73.67284,45.48758.status: Certificate of GAP Last visit: interim, January 2026
-73.67284,45.48758.desc: An institution certified by the Canadian Council on Animal Care for its use of animals in science. A site of National Research Council Canada. Certificate of GAP Last visit: interim, January 2026. CCAC certification is a condition of federal research funding rather than a licence, so an institution outside it is not necessarily outside the work — it may simply not take federal money. The CCAC publishes names and certificate status and no addresses, so this point marks the institution rather than the building where animals are held.

-71.60774,-33.05224.name: Clinica de Reproduccion Humana de la Universidad de Valparaiso
-71.60774,-33.05224.desc: A centre accredited by REDLARA, the Latin American Network of Assisted Reproduction. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. REDLARA accreditation is voluntary and its members report to a shared registry, which is why Latin America can be read at all — most countries in the region have no national register of clinics. What it is not is a complete list: a clinic outside REDLARA appears nowhere.

-76.98220,39.03490.name: Cooper Surgical — culture media recall
-76.98220,39.03490.desc: The 2024 recall of IVF culture media after embryos failed to develop, with litigation following from families whose cycles were lost. The media is regulated as a device rather than as the environment an embryo develops in, and the difference determines what testing was required beforehand.

-76.98220,39.03490.name: Jesse Gelsinger and the 1999 trial death — FDA record
-76.98220,39.03490.desc: An eighteen-year-old died in a gene therapy trial in 1999, and the investigation found undisclosed conflicts of interest and unreported adverse events in earlier patients. The field stalled for a decade. The records are the reason trial registration and conflict disclosure exist in their current form.

-76.98220,39.03490.name: Cure Rare Disease and the 2022 trial death
-76.98220,39.03490.desc: A patient died in 2022 in a custom gene therapy trial built for his own single mutation, funded and organised by a non-profit his brother founded. Bespoke therapies for one person sidestep the economics that make ultra-rare disease untreatable, and they also sidestep the accumulated safety evidence that comes from treating many patients with the same product. This is the case the whole n-of-one field is measured against.

5.11000,52.09000.name: Topigs Norsvin
5.11000,52.09000.desc: A Dutch-Norwegian pig genetics company supplying breeding stock across Europe, the Americas and Asia, and one of the three companies that between them supply most of the world's commercial pig genetics. It runs genomic selection and computed-tomography scanning of breeding animals, and has worked on editing for disease resistance. Pigs are the animal where editing is furthest advanced in food production and also the source of engineered organs for human transplant, so the same breeding companies sit behind both.
